questions.q: Per this lesson, how does compliance differ from governance?
options: Compliance is meeting specific, externally mandated legal requirements; governance is the broader internal discipline that includes but extends beyond legal minimums
They are exactly the same thing with different names
Compliance only applies to Salesforce, while governance applies to every other system
Governance is a subset of compliance
questions.explain: The lesson describes compliance as governance's legal floor, not its ceiling -- an org can be fully compliant yet still have ungoverned data in areas the law doesn't touch.

questions.q: Which data-subject right does this lesson describe as essentially a normal data-quality workflow (from Chapter 1) applied to one named individual's records under a deadline?
options: Right to erasure
Right to data portability
Right to rectification
Right of access
questions.explain: The lesson frames the right to rectification (correcting inaccurate data) as the same kind of work Chapter 1's data-quality lessons already cover, just applied to a specific person on a deadline.

questions.q: What limitation does this lesson identify with treating "delete the Contact record" as the whole job of an erasure request?
options: Deleting a Contact record is technically impossible in Salesforce
Erasure requests can only ever apply to Lead records, never Contacts
Erasure automatically deletes every related record across every connected system with no further action needed

Related records (Cases, Opportunities, custom-object children) may still reference the person and need separate handling, and deletion doesn't automatically propagate to downstream systems like a marketing platform or a backup snapshot
questions.explain: The lesson stresses that a real erasure process has to account for related records and for every downstream system the data was synced to, since Salesforce deletion doesn't automatically reach those other places.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say industry-specific regulations like HIPAA or SOX can create tension with an individual's erasure request?
options: They often require retention periods measured in years, which directly conflicts with a request to delete that same data -- a conflict that has to be resolved by policy, not improvised case by case
They never apply to the same records, so there's no real tension
HIPAA and SOX both require immediate deletion of all records upon any request
These regulations only apply to companies outside the United States
questions.explain: Industry-specific recordkeeping obligations can require years of retention, directly in tension with erasure requests -- the same conflict Lesson 6 covers for retention policy generally.

questions.q: What does this lesson say is wrong with treating "we're compliant" as a permanent, one-time certification?
options: Nothing is wrong with it -- compliance never needs to be reassessed once achieved

Regulations change, and new objects, integrations, or AI features (like a Data Cloud rollout) can introduce new personal-data processing that was never formally assessed -- compliance needs a recurring review with a named owner, like classification or data quality
Only external auditors are allowed to reassess compliance, so internal teams should never try
Compliance certificates issued by regulators never expire under any law
questions.explain: The lesson explicitly compares compliance to classification and data quality: all three need a recurring review cadence and a named owner rather than being treated as permanently settled.
